topic: writers and authors trying to get AI to write in their own voice instead of generic AI prose
blind_spots: Almost no evidence on cost, pricing, or willingness to pay for voice-preserving tools.
No quantified data on time-savings vs. quality trade-offs beyond anecdotes ('5 minutes', '15 minutes').
Little on non-fiction/business writing, screenwriting, or non-English-language writers; sample skews to fiction, poetry, and essays.
No evidence comparing specific tools/models head-to-head on voice fidelity.
No longitudinal data on whether calibration techniques actually sustain voice across a full manuscript.
Reader/audience perspective on detecting voice is asserted by writers but not validated by reader-side evidence.
contradictions: Some writers insist AI prose is 'really obvious' and easy to detect, while others fear genuine human work will be falsely flagged as AI — implying detection is unreliable.

One camp treats AI voice failure as an inherent, accepted limitation (novelist 'accepted that as a limitation'), while tutorials claim adequate context/calibration makes output sound human ('nobody's calling your book robotic').
The 'AI ruins writing' sentiment is framed as a serious craft/ethics threat by some, but dismissed as 'noise' getting 'old fast' by others in the same community.
Critics frame AI users as 'not real writers,' yet the same evidence set includes writers actively using AI and seeking to make it work in their voice.
